quarterly_data.signal: CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
quarterly_data.figure: Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — PHOTONICS: A $10B MAP BY 2030, AND THE LTA MODEL: Corning's new PHOTONICS Market-Access Platform targets $10 BILLION of revenue by 2030 — passive photonics INSIDE THE BOX (FAU harnesses and everything that moves/manages light between the faceplate and the silicon-photonics optical engine) for CPO/NPO, where Corning historically had ZERO content; likely starts with scale-out, and optical SCALE-UP supercharges it; the plan is built on 'assumptions and discussions AND AGREEMENTS with customers.' Despite industry chatter on scale-up timing, 'NO CHANGES to our fundamental belief... inside the real ecosystem there is much less drama than what it looks like from outside.' Business model: long-term agreements (Amazon multi-billion, NVIDIA, Meta up-to-$6B, Apple) will be 'the LION'S SHARE of our optical business' — every major capacity expansion is underpinned by risk/reward-sharing LTAs; profitability comes from innovation value-share, not bare-fiber pricing (optical NI +77% to a record 21% margin). Springboard math: run rate $20B by end-2026 (Q3 guide may hit it a QUARTER EARLY) -> $30B (2028) -> $40B (2030), 19% CAGR; high-confidence variant $27B/$35B; biggest risk-adjustment between the two = SCALE-UP TIMING. Elsewhere: memory prices push handsets down mid-teens % (Gorilla outperforms on content) but push TVs LARGER/premium (favors Gen 10.5); solar recovers from Q3 toward a $3B stream, with MORE POLYSILICON SHIFTING TO SEMICONDUCTOR (ELECTRONIC) GRADE at Hemlock; FY capex ~$2B.
quarterly_data.figure: Photonics MAP = $10B by 2030 (inside-the-box passive, zero prior content); LTAs = lion's share of optical; $20B run rate possibly a qtr early

quarterly_data.signal: New named customer announced the day before the conference: a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar deal with Verizon to help build out a new long-haul network that supports both Verizon's broadband business and data center interconnect. Corning has supplied Verizon for 30 years. Schlesinger grouped Verizon with the extended Lumen agreement and the previously announced Zayo agreement as the three deals now carrying the DCI business, and said the same fully connectorized solution logic applies to Verizon's fiber-to-the-home build.
quarterly_data.figure: multi-year, multi-billion-dollar deal with Verizon; 30 years as a Verizon supplier

quarterly_data.signal: Data center interconnect pulled forward: Corning had previously shared that DCI was about a $1 billion opportunity, $1 billion a year by the end of the decade. With the Lumen extension, the Zayo agreement and the new Verizon deal, management now expects to reach that number much sooner than the end of the decade and believes the opportunity is bigger than that, with an update to follow. Corning's dense fiber cables — more fibers in the same cable diameter — are the reason it is winning DCI, and are what it sells Lumen.
quarterly_data.figure: DCI $1 billion a year by the end of the decade now expected much sooner than the end of the decade and bigger than that

quarterly_data.signal: Quarter-to-date update, six weeks after the Q2 call: Corning expects to deliver the $20 billion annualized run rate a quarter early, in the third quarter, which puts sales at the high end or slightly better than the guidance given back in July. The third quarter is running really well and the fourth quarter is expected to be bigger than the third, with the high teens year-over-year growth seen in Q2 and Q3 continuing into Q4 and into next year. The $30 billion by end-2028 and $40 billion by end-2030 Springboard targets were explicitly NOT upgraded today, though management says deals like Verizon give more confidence in reaching the upper bound and maybe beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: $20 billion run rate a quarter early in Q3; sales at the high end or slightly better than July guidance; high teens YoY growth continuing into Q4 and next year; $30 billion / $40 billion targets unchanged

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and constraints: Corning is not fiber constrained today but expects to be, which is why it committed to significantly increase US fiber capacity at what it calls the world's largest, lowest-cost fiber factory; that capacity starts coming online in the not that distant future and is tied to customer agreements. Cable and connectivity capacity has been added quarter over quarter for close to a year, and connectivity is where Corning expects to be most constrained relative to today's capacity as scale-up drives growth. Customers are funding part of the build through deposits they earn back by purchasing, and Corning modularises capacity adds rather than bringing on a whole factory at a time.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics timing sharpened: Corning is planning to build out a $10 billion business by the end of the decade, from no sales today, selling into NPO and CPO applications inside the server tray, and is building out the supply chain now — hopefully next year we will start to see some sales there. The single biggest variable for the Springboard high-confidence gap is CPO adoption; the CPO supply chain at the scale required does not exist today and is the largest build investors should watch, though management sees no showstopper. Schlesinger expects the adoption inflection in the next four or five years rather than in 2027, with near-term content coming from traditional product sets (polarization-maintaining fiber, FAUs) and GlassBridge-type products a 2030-plus opportunity. Scale-up of the network should begin at the end of next year and run 2028 through 2030; today's growth is scale-out, where clusters above 130,000 GPUs add another network layer.
quarterly_data.figure: $10 billion photonics business by the end of the decade from no sales today; first sales hoped for next year; adoption inflection in the next four or five years, not 2027; 130,000 cluster barometer

quarterly_data.signal: CPO / ultra-high-power lasers: lead CPO customers' production plans 'remain very much on track, and their demand signal has increased since our last update.' Lumentum remains confident in an ultra-high-power laser chip demand ramp in the second half of calendar 2027, ahead of customer scale-up deployments in calendar 2028. Because the first phase of scale-up optical connections spans across compute racks within a cluster, the ramp applies to any topology larger than one rack. Ultra-high-power laser revenue is expected to reach roughly the $50 million mark by the end of calendar 2026, with the first triple-digit ($100M+) quarter expected in fiscal Q3 FY2027.
quarterly_data.figure: UHP laser ramp H2 CY2027 for CY2028 scale-up; ~$50M by end CY2026; first $100M+ quarter fiscal Q3 FY2027

quarterly_data.signal: First external light source (ELS) MODULE purchase order received, for delivery by the second half of calendar 2027 - Lumentum's first move up the stack from selling laser chips into selling the full ELS module. ASP is 'meaningfully higher than the set of lasers that we ship in'; module margins are above corporate average but below the laser chips, a deliberate trade of some margin for revenue acceleration. Wupen Yuen: the ELS module is positioned to enable 'customers who don't know how to deal with individual laser chips' to build CPO and NPO systems.
quarterly_data.figure: first ELS module purchase order (delivery H2 CY2027); ASP meaningfully higher than laser set

quarterly_data.signal: NPO (near-packaged optics) called 'completely additive' and 'significantly increasing the optical TAM.' The rest of the customer base beyond the lead CPO account is prioritizing NPO as an intermediate step to eventual CPO adoption; even the largest CPO customer is evaluating NPO for specific new use cases. Two laser types are being evaluated for NPO: a mid-power laser integrated directly into the optical engine, and a high-power laser in an external light source module. Lumentum's NPO/CPO laser family spans 120 mW, 150 mW, and 400 mW output levels off common design and process know-how. Wupen Yuen: each NPO set carries ~6.4T of bandwidth, roughly four times a local module, and NPO should hit the market in the late 2027 / 2028 timeframe to enable optical scale-up.
quarterly_data.figure: NPO additive to optical TAM; 120/150/400 mW laser family; ~6.4T per NPO set; market late 2027-2028

quarterly_data.signal: Supply-demand imbalance update: no change on EMLs (still shipping behind customer demand, previously cited at greater than 30%), but high-powered lasers have deteriorated sharply - 'we are way behind in our shipments... The demand signal has increased, and we are very much further behind relative to our ability to supply.' Management clarified the ramp execution itself is on track; the gap widened because demand accelerated. High-powered lasers were named as the one vector that materially changed since the prior quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: EML imbalance unchanged (>30%); high-power laser shortfall materially worse on accelerating demand

quarterly_data.signal: EMLs delivered another record-breaking quarter, primarily driven by 100G-per-lane devices. 200G EMLs are accelerating and now account for over 25% of total EML revenue; management expects 200G EMLs to be 50% or more of volume by mid-calendar-2027. Lumentum remains on track to deliver over 50% EML unit growth in the December 2026 quarter versus the year-ago quarter, but expects to remain significantly behind demand even at year end.
quarterly_data.figure: record EML quarter; 200G EML >25% of EML revenue; >50% EML unit growth by Dec-2026 quarter

quarterly_data.signal: CW laser strategy expanded materially. The new 200G-per-lane CW laser chip has a significantly reduced die size, is more efficient, and delivers margins accretive to long-term financial targets; Lumentum is commanding a significant price premium versus market price because tight spec width produces superior transceiver yields at customers. The margin gap between CW and EML 'has closed considerably' since the prior call (EML still better). Better-than-expected output in Japan is being allocated to CW, and Lumentum is now shipping CW lasers in a relatively meaningful way into the 200G-per-lane silicon photonics opportunity, on top of internal deployment in its own transceivers.
quarterly_data.figure: 200G CW laser: smaller die, price premium, margin gap to EML closed considerably

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity: expanding across the two indium phosphide wafer fabs in Japan to capture coming 200G and 300G lane-speed opportunities, qualifying both CW and EML process flows on the newest tools as they come online. Demand for both EML and CW lasers is expected to grow significantly through the second half of calendar 2026 and into 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: two Japan InP fabs expanding; CW and EML flows qualifying on new tools

quarterly_data.signal: Pump lasers: shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year and Lumentum will 'remain effectively sold out for the foreseeable future despite our rapid capacity expansion.' A fourfold increase in pump laser shipments is still expected over the next several quarters. Share is roughly 70%-80%. Capacity is ramping at Rose Orchard (US) with packaging and test in Thailand. Multiple long-term customer agreements have been secured to help offset planned capital expenditures - mostly three-year arrangements with built-in pricing levers and, in most instances, take-or-pay structures, formed largely with NEMs (network equipment manufacturers).
quarterly_data.figure: pump lasers +80% YoY; 4x shipment increase expected; ~70-80% share; 3-year take-or-pay LTAs

quarterly_data.signal: Narrow linewidth laser assembly shipments grew sequentially for the 10th consecutive quarter and were up over 130% year-over-year. Scale-across demand is being driven by inferencing and training applications requiring full-rate connectivity between data centers, plus political and regulatory constraints favoring smaller, more modular builds. Scale of the DCI opportunity: for one major hyperscaler, the network capacity connecting just two AI data center sites is double the total global backbone capacity that hyperscaler built over the entirety of the last decade.
quarterly_data.figure: narrow linewidth +130% YoY, 10th consecutive sequential growth quarter

quarterly_data.signal: Cloud transceivers: record 800G shipments in the quarter while initiating production of next-generation 1.6T modules. Transceiver profitability continues to improve on yield gains, capacity utilization, and the initial rollout of higher-ASP 1.6T units. 1.6T uptake is expected to intensify starting in fiscal Q1 FY2027 and sustain through calendar 2027, anchored by lead Tier 1 hyperscale customers rolling out custom AI clusters. Management believes Lumentum is first to market ahead of larger competitors in many instances and can hold that share advantage through the cycle, crediting its signal integrity team on difficult 1.6T designs.
quarterly_data.figure: record 800G shipments; 1.6T production initiated; 1.6T uptake intensifies from fiscal Q1 FY2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS: shipments doubled from fiscal Q3 to fiscal Q4, and Q1 FY2027 guidance includes Lumentum's first triple-digit OCS revenue quarter - expected to be 'meaningfully above the three-digit mark' ($100M+). Tracking to (not ahead of) the previously stated $400 million of OCS shipments for the second half of calendar 2026, leaving room to run in the fourth calendar quarter. Demand signal for 2027 'continues to be incredibly strong'; initial work started to add capacity with contract manufacturers alongside increasing internal factory output. Lumentum describes itself as the only merchant OCS supplier with a shipping track record, and expects to cross over to become the number one OCS supplier sometime in early 2027 versus one customer's internal source of supply.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS shipments 2x QoQ; first $100M+ OCS quarter guided; $400M H2 CY2026 on track; #1 supplier expected early 2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS roadmap broadened since the prior call: Lumentum is now planning higher and lower port count products, including specialized in-tray offerings. These are entirely additive to the TAM presented at OFC and are expected to hit in the 2028 timeframe, requiring significant engineering redesign.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS in-tray and higher/lower port-count products; additive TAM; 2028 timeframe

quarterly_data.signal: Greensboro, North Carolina fab (fifth InP fab, acquired March 2026): conversion from gallium arsenide to indium phosphide is 'well underway,' with long-pole items such as reactors already addressed. No change to schedule - first revenue in early 2028, ramping through calendar 2028 to full pitch by end of 2028 and into 2029. Capacity remains uncommitted and Lumentum is actively talking to customers about laser demand, expecting to announce new Greensboro arrangements (LTAs) over the next couple of quarters.
quarterly_data.figure: Greensboro GaAs-to-InP conversion underway; first revenue early 2028; ramp into 2029; LTAs in discussion

quarterly_data.signal: InP substrate supply: after a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand across a couple of customers, Lumentum spent the last three months securing additional substrate supply and signed a deal with AXT during the quarter. Hurlston: 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner.' Lumentum is comfortable near-term on the strength of its lead arrangement with a Japanese supplier plus the AXT deal, but flagged that given the rate of change in the demand vector 'that may not be true a quarter or two from now either' - more substrate help is likely needed if the vector continues.
quarterly_data.figure: AXT InP substrate deal signed in Q4; more substrate supply likely needed if demand vector continues

quarterly_data.signal: Technology roadmap view: silicon photonics is a viable solution at 1.6T and CW lasers are taking a significant portion of transceiver output, but at 3.2T silicon photonics 'loses some of its advantages' and Lumentum expects EMLs to come back in a meaningful way. Wupen Yuen added that in a supply-constrained environment customers will use whichever laser source they can get, so the EML-versus-CW mix is a supply/demand dynamic as much as a technical one. CPO remains the natural end state - optics placed directly on the substrate or interposer for maximum power efficiency through foundry-level advanced packaging.
quarterly_data.figure: SiPho viable at 1.6T; EML expected to return at 3.2T; CPO the end state via foundry advanced packaging

quarterly_data.signal: Competitive: on Chinese companies bringing new indium phosphide fabs to market, Hurlston said 'we obviously haven't seen any impact on our numbers as yet. I don't expect there to be any impact,' citing EML differentiation, high/mid-power laser differentiation for NPO and CPO, and an ability to price up even in CW because tight spec consistency drives superior customer transceiver yields. He cautioned that some Chinese laser suppliers are not yet delivering into the market.
quarterly_data.figure: no impact seen from new Chinese InP fabs; price premium sustained

quarterly_data.signal: Adjacent businesses: industrial lasers and cable access strengthened quarter-over-quarter. Within industrial lasers, increased adoption of ultrafast lasers targeting high-density PCB via drilling that supports advanced AI XPU boards and 1.6T optical modules. In 3D sensing, Lumentum has visibility to an expanding set of applications expected to drive growth in upcoming product cycles with its primary customer.
quarterly_data.figure: ultrafast lasers for AI XPU board / 1.6T module PCB via drilling; expanding 3D sensing pipeline

quarterly_data.signal: Named by AOI management on its Q2 FY2026 call as one of the very few suppliers able to serve the high-power CPO laser market: AOI, Lumentum, Coherent and Broadcom are all 'invest[ing] huge money' in laser capacity, yet 'even combined... it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years'. Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.
quarterly_data.figure: Industry high-power laser capacity must grow 8-10x for CPO; 21-24 month equipment lead time

We started with customers other than Google... we actually have customers that were much more substantial than Google in our early rounds of shipments.' One of the more interesting emerging use cases is deploying an OCS inside the rack itself, one per rack, to route around GPUs or TPUs that have failed or are overloaded - a surprising number of GPUs in a data center fail, and a compute model can represent '$20, 30, $40 million of compute time'. quarterly_data.signal: New EML economics and share math. Moving from 100G to 200G EML gives 'about a 2x uplift in price' - ASPs roughly double - and 200G lasers arrive at the 1.6T node. At 200G there is 'very little competition': Broadcom is a supplier of 200G EMLs, Lumentum is the other large supplier, and management sees no other entrants soon. On mix, EML-based transceivers are 'probably 70%-80%' of the 800G market but are expected to be only '40%-50% of the market at 1.6T' as silicon photonics takes share, so raw EML units go up while share comes down. At 3.2T Lumentum's transceiver engineers say 'silicon photonics again runs out of steam', producing 'a double whammy' where both EML unit numbers and EML share rise. Hurlston also framed the yield argument behind the price premium: the tolerance of the laser sets transceiver yield more than anything else, so a higher laser price 'more than makes up for itself in the high yields'.

quarterly_data.signal: NPO timing moved materially since the earnings call: 'prior to our last earnings call, we probably thought that it was going to be a late 2028 into early 2029 event... It seems like now it's a late 2027 into early 2028 event', because customers competing with NVIDIA concluded they need to deploy a lot more optics and to do so sooner. Hurlston called the near-term NPO opportunity larger than the CPO opportunity, with a higher adoption rate of optical lanes than NVIDIA's, and said NPO customers are requiring Lumentum to ship the entire ELS rather than bare laser chips. The consequence is capacity: NPO 'is going to put a lot of pressure on that Greensboro fab', Lumentum needs a 'next leg of the stool' and is trying to lock up NPO business now to fill Greensboro and more, but would require an NVIDIA-style commitment before funding further capacity. NVIDIA underwrote Greensboro with a long-term agreement characterised as a multibillion-dollar deal plus an investment that helped Lumentum buy, equip and outfit the fab, acquired early calendar 2026 and not operational until early calendar 2028; the team running it was inherited from Qorvo, and qualification at NVIDIA itself took a year.

The reverse risk is tit-for-tat curtailment of Chinese sub-component supply - substrates, isolators and other raw materials Lumentum currently relies on - against which its manufacturing footprint in Thailand, in China itself and in the United Kingdom (a safe harbour on substrates) is the hedge.

Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.

Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.

quarterly_data.signal: Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE, described as the industry's first OCI MSA compatible solution for near and co-packaged optics, has 7 ACTIVE ENGAGEMENTS with leading companies. GF taped out a SCALE-related design win in Q2 and expects to tape out another in Q3. Management reiterated a consistent timeline: the NPO ramp BEGINS IN 2027 and the CPO ramp BEGINS IN 2028. Because near and co-packaged optics are built on a common photonic IC - an EIC bonded to a PIC with a micro-optic and a fiber-attached unit - and differ mainly in that NPO is bonded to the board while CPO sits within the package (plus SerDes architecture differences), GF expects to benefit regardless of which form factor customers adopt. Many customers are pursuing both, with NPO ramping sooner. Breen attributed the sudden industry interest in NPO to SerDes synergies that make the system transition smaller than a jump straight to full CPO, and expects pluggables, NPO and CPO all to coexist in the data center.

quarterly_data.signal: GF entered a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a $300 MILLION award to accelerate next-generation silicon photonics technologies in the U.S. The funding supports three components: continued PIC-level innovation and improved modulator technology to reach 400-gig per lane and beyond; NEW MATERIALS to be introduced into the system - management named barium titanate, thin-film lithium niobate and indium phosphide; and packaging capability and capacity for the integrated optical engines needed for near and co-packaged optics, building directly on the SCALE platform. Management said the endorsement came from the world's top XPU providers, hyperscalers, AI connectivity leaders and ecosystem partners.
quarterly_data.figure: $300M U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for next-generation silicon photonics

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon germanium is OVERSUBSCRIBED THROUGHOUT 2027 and, notably, GF's SiGe business is LARGER THAN ITS SILICON PHOTONICS BUSINESS TODAY. GF secured multiple new SiGe TIA and driver design wins across networking customers in the quarter. The growth has two compounding drivers: the shift to optical networking itself, and the fact that what could previously be done in CMOS at 50-gig and 100-gig per lane cannot be done at 200-gig and definitely not at 400-gig per lane, forcing transimpedance amplifiers and increasingly the drivers out into high-performance analog processes like SiGe. High-performance analog also appears in near and co-packaged optics depending on architecture. GF is expanding SiGe capacity at Burlington, Vermont and qualifying 300-millimeter SiGe in Singapore for additional capacity, better economics and higher fT/fMAX performance. The SiGe lineage traces to IBM Microelectronics, which invented SiGe and is part of GF today.
quarterly_data.figure: SiGe oversubscribed throughout 2027; SiGe business larger than silicon photonics today; Vermont capacity expanding, 300mm SiGe qualifying in Singapore

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity strategy is a structural advantage: GF is adding capacity WITHIN ITS EXISTING FAB FOOTPRINT rather than building new fabs, which management contrasted with competitors on longer lead times. Breen said GF 'could 10x our photonics capacity within our current 4 walls' globally on its long-term plan. Q2 utilization was in the high 80s, leaving about 10 points of headroom to grow into with installed capacity. Confidence in bringing capacity online plus factory productivity improvements was cited as a direct contributor to raising the full-year CID outlook. On competition in silicon photonics, Breen said customers are coming to GF saying they do not have enough capacity secured and want more, partly to mitigate geopolitical risk, and he sees no customer-concentration concern given 40-plus customers.

quarterly_data.signal: GF launched Quantum Technology Solutions in May 2026, a dedicated team aimed at taking the quantum industry from prototypes to high-volume production. The strategy is qubit-agnostic across superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological and spin modalities, using the FDX platform as a cryogenic CMOS foundation and extending advanced packaging into the cryogenic regime for 3D heterogeneous integration. GF is working with 8 of the world's leading quantum computing players including PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Quantum Motion plus endorsements from the quantum arms of large hyperscalers, and has already begun 4 new customer-specific engagements in the three months since launch. The effort is anchored by an expected $375 MILLION grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Over the next 1 to 3 years quantum revenue comes largely through engineering engagements booked in technology services, with manufacturing-services revenue ramping toward the end of the decade. Several quantum players are working on the photonics side of their solutions, which maps directly onto GF's silicon photonics roadmap.
quarterly_data.figure: $375M expected U.S. Department of Commerce quantum grant; 8 leading quantum players engaged; 4 new customer engagements in 3 months

quarterly_data.signal: IP, software and custom silicon: GF completed the acquisition of the Synopsys ARC processor IP Solutions business in June, adding CPU, DSP, NPU and RISC-V technologies, a software development toolkit and application-specific processor design capability - over 150 patents, 300 existing customers and 400 R&D engineers. Combined with MIPS, this lets GF engage customers earlier in the design cycle for edge AI and on-device inference in automotive, industrial and robotics. Full-year 2026 technology services contribution from MIPS plus ARC was RAISED to $100-120 million from a prior $60-100 million, skewed roughly one third Q3 and two thirds Q4, and technology services revenue is now expected toward the high end of the 10-12% of total revenue range with gross margin significantly above corporate targets. Design wins in the quarter included 3 strategic chiplet wins with Lockheed Martin on FinFET and FDX, an expanded FinFET win with Microchip, a first-ever PMIC design win with MediaTek on the BCD platform, an ADAS radar tape-out for Bosch on FDX, and a new microLED display backplane win for augmented reality wearables at a leading hyperscaler.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.

On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.

We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. contracts.signal: CEO Bill Brennan: 'Our first customer, Microsoft, the reason that they converted to AECs was really the functionality that we offered' — Credo developed a solution smart enough to sense when a TOR port was failing or about to fail and switch the data to a redundant TOR in a hitless manner; recounted as the origin of the AEC category whose playbook Credo is now applying to ZeroFlap Optics.

contracts.signal: CEO Bill Brennan named xAI as the customer that created the ZeroFlap concept: while building in another data center xAI was 'struggling mightily with link flaps' and could not keep cluster availability above even 90%. Moving into its own liquid-cooled data center, 'they came to us and said... What we want you to do is extend your AEC family from 3 meters to 7 meters because if you can do 7 meters, we can cover every connection in the row, and we can build a ZeroFlap cluster.' Brennan notes this is the ONLY transition where copper has replaced optical, for lengths up to 7 meters. He visited Memphis over the summer: xAI has achieved 99.9% uptime and can bring a cluster up in 5 days versus 6 to 8 weeks.
contracts.units: AEC family extended from 3 meters to 7 meters

connects_to.relationship: ZeroFlap Optics with real-time link telemetry for NIC-to-first-switch connections longer than 7 meters

contracts.signal: Oracle named as the customer behind the telemetry version of ZeroFlap: 'After we made this transition, Oracle came to us and said, Look, we'd love to address these problems as well, but our connections between the NIC and the first switch are longer than 7 meters, and we can't redesign. We've got what we've got.' Credo designed a custom DSP plus a software platform that lights up continuous real-time telemetry on each of the six links between a GPU and a switch (three in each direction), measuring eye height, SNR, post-FEC bit error rates and histograms to create a yellow 'check engine light' for a link instead of only green or red; it also identifies multipath interference caused by dust on the fiber plant and latent ESD damage, and mitigates likely link flaps by taking a link down in an orderly way rather than disrupting the cluster.

It describes the architectural evolution as pluggable transceivers with DSPs, to LPO platforms that remove the DSP, morphing into smaller package-less NPO platforms; those architectures still need drivers and TIAs, but with much higher density - smaller parts, more channels, lower power, and varied form factors using wire bonds, bumped devices or flip chip, plus through-silicon-via options. quarterly_data.signal: CALL — OPEN CPO STANCE AND THE SCALE-UP VIEW: scale-up philosophy = 'COPPER IF YOU CAN, OPTICS IF YOU MUST.' Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' Scale-up positioning: 'we live in an NVIDIA world' — where NVIDIA supplies the full NVLink vertical stack there is little Arista participation (Arista wins scale-out/across), but for NON-NVIDIA accelerators (AMD MI series, Google TPUs — 'increasingly a FORMIDABLE training processor', in-house XPUs, inference chips) Arista works BOTH scale-up and scale-out, including CUSTOM RACKS tuned to customers' engines; 'feels like InfiniBand 2-3 years ago... it will take time to move from proprietary NVLink to alternatives, even if Ethernet's really good — I expect us to do much better there.' 1.6T cadence (history repeats 800G's trials-2023/24 -> ramp-2025/26): TRIALS H2 2026 with single-digit VERY LARGE customers; REAL PRODUCTION 2027 (liquid-cooling infrastructure required). EOS innovations for AI fabrics: SSU hitless upgrades, MRC packet-spray/reassembly (kills hash-collision slowdowns), SRv6 explicit-path load balancing with real-time congestion signals — one binary from scale-out to scale-across.

The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. Arista builds CPO or NPO switches when customers ask; XPO timing is partly aligned with scale-up form factor and bandwidth density needs.

Framework: scale-up splits into proprietary (NVLink and UALink), a commodity white-box play for lower value-add needs, and value-add Ethernet where Arista plays - with the open question being how much of the TAM Ethernet starts at and whether proprietary migrates to Ethernet as InfiniBand did. quarterly_data.signal: AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.
quarterly_data.figure: Hundreds of IC pinouts per tray; hyperscalers ~10% of revenue direct; chiplet + workload emulation
